title: Manus Raises Over $500 Million in First Round Since Meta Breakup
excerpt: Butterfly Effect's AI agent startup, unwound from Meta's $2 billion-plus acquisition by Beijing in April, now has fresh capital and a reported $500 million revenue run rate.
body:
• Butterfly Effect, the parent company of AI startup Manus, has completed a funding round of more than $500 million — its first raise since unwinding Meta's $2 billion-plus acquisition earlier this year.
  • The round was co-led by Boyu Capital and IDG Capital, with Tencent, Sequoia China and ZhenFund also participating, according to CNBC.
  • Beijing ordered Meta to unwind the acquisition in April amid tightening scrutiny of US investment in Chinese advanced-AI startups; Manus resumed independent operations in August.
  • The Information reported Manus's annualised revenue run rate has surged to about $500 million, up from $100 million when Meta bought it — a sign the general-purpose AI agent bet is generating real commercial demand.

Independence, funded

Manus, the AI startup that became the centre of a geopolitical tug-of-war this spring, is back on its own feet — and investors have responded with a cheque worth more than $500 million.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=XKvibQQSyjU

"The Information reported in June that Manus's annualised revenue run rate had surged to about $500 million, up from roughly $100 million when Meta acquired it."

Butterfly Effect, Manus's parent company, said on Thursday it had completed the funding round as the firm resumed independent operations after unwinding Meta's acquisition, which was valued at more than $2 billion. The round was co-led by Boyu Capital and IDG Capital, with existing investors Tencent, Sequoia China and ZhenFund participating, CNBC reported.

Manus builds general-purpose AI agents — software that can autonomously carry out tasks such as research and automation with minimal human input. The category has become one of the most fiercely contested in technology, with the biggest US labs racing to move beyond chatbots into agents that can actually do work.

The unwinding

In April, Beijing ordered Meta to unwind its acquisition of Manus amid tightening scrutiny of US investment in Chinese startups developing advanced AI technologies. The intervention underscored how AI dealmaking now sits squarely inside great-power competition: a transaction that would once have been a straightforward tech acquisition became a test case for China's outbound-investment controls.

https://x.com/kevin980606/status/2108450078637830159

Manus said in August that it would resume operating as an independent company and delete some user data as part of its separation from Meta — a clean break designed to satisfy regulators on both sides.

Revenue is the real story

What makes the raise notable is what happened between the acquisition and the unwind. The Information reported in June that Manus's annualised revenue run rate had surged to about $500 million, up from roughly $100 million when Meta acquired it. For an AI agent company, that is the number that matters: it suggests enterprises are paying real money for autonomous agents, not merely experimenting with them.

The same report said Manus was considering a joint-venture structure incorporated in China, a path that could pave the way for a Hong Kong listing — positioning the company for the capital markets rather than another sale.

What it means for the AI race

Manus's trajectory captures the strange new shape of the AI industry: a Chinese-born startup, briefly owned by an American giant, now funded by Chinese and global capital to compete with everyone. The agent race is no longer an American monopoly, and investors are pricing that in.

For Indian technology watchers, the Manus story lands in a familiar frame. India's global capability centres have become a crucial delivery engine for exactly this kind of enterprise AI work, and the country's IT services giants are all racing to productise agentic AI. A half-billion-dollar vote of confidence in AI agents is, by extension, a vote of confidence in the market India serves.

What's next

Watch the product. Manus's valuation case now rests on converting that $500 million revenue run rate into durable growth — and on whether general-purpose agents can cross from impressive demos to mission-critical enterprise software. A Hong Kong listing would be the next public milestone, and Beijing's tolerance for the company's ambitions will remain the quiet variable behind everything it does.
